opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things that really motivates a lot of my work. What strikes me is that infants seem to build a surprisingly rich understanding of the world well before they have any language to hang it on. There are these classic studies, the violation-of-expectation experiments, where you show a young infant a scene that breaks some basic physical regularity. An object passes through a solid wall, or something seems to vanish when it's occluded, or a toy appears to float unsupported. The infants look longer at those impossible events. That suggests they've already formed expectations about object permanence, solidity, continuity, even some intuitive notion of gravity and support, and it's happening within the first several months of life.

What I find compelling is how they're learning it. Nobody is giving them labels. There's no supervision in the sense we usually mean in machine learning. They're mostly just observing, and to some extent interacting, and building an internal model of how things tend to unfold. Then when something deviates from what that model predicts, it registers as surprise. So there's this picture of learning as prediction in some abstract space, where you're not trying to reconstruct every pixel of what you see. You're learning which aspects of the world are predictable and actually matter.

That maps quite directly onto the questions we're asking in self-supervised learning. A lot of current AI, especially large language models, gets its knowledge from text, which is an enormously compressed, human-curated signal. Children show you can get a lot of grounded common sense before language even enters the picture, and language then gets layered on top of concepts that already exist. That makes me think that if we want systems with real physical understanding, and the ability to plan and reason about the consequences of actions, we probably need them to learn the way infants do, from raw sensory streams like video, by predicting abstract representations of what comes next or what's missing.

It also gives us a nice way to evaluate models. You can borrow the violation-of-expectation paradigm directly. Show a model physically plausible and implausible videos and see whether its prediction error, its "surprise," is higher for the impossible ones. That's a much more cognitively grounded test than many standard benchmarks. Seeing that kind of intuitive physics emerge purely from self-supervised pretraining on natural video, without hard-coding any of those priors, tells you something about which ingredients are actually necessary.

So for me the developmental literature does two things. It's an existence proof that this kind of learning is possible, and it's a source of concrete hypotheses and experiments we can use to check whether our models are moving in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response says infants build an understanding of the world before language and lists physical concepts such as object permanence, solidity, continuity, and gravity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think what's really striking is that, if you look at the work of people like Elizabeth Spelke or Renée Baillargeon, they show that infants, really within the first few months of life, already have a pretty rich model of how the physical world works. They understand things like object permanence, that objects don't just blink out of existence when they're occluded. They have expectations about solidity, that one object can't pass through another, about gravity, that unsupported things fall, about continuity of motion. And they test this with these very clever violation-of-expectation experiments, where you show the baby something that's physically impossible, and they look longer at it, because it surprises them.

And what's interesting to me, from the machine learning side, is that all of this is happening before language, before any explicit supervision. Nobody is sitting there labeling the world for the infant and saying, "this is an object, this is support, this is occlusion." They're essentially just observing. They're watching a stream of sensory input, and from that they're acquiring these abstract concepts, these intuitive physics priors that then become the foundation for everything that comes after.

So if you contrast that with how we've traditionally trained models, where so much of the progress has come from either enormous amounts of labeled data, or from language, which is really a kind of compressed, already-abstracted representation of the world that humans produced, it raises this question of what is the learning principle that lets you get those concepts directly from raw observation. Because clearly it's possible, biology is an existence proof. And I think the answer has something to do with prediction. The child is constantly forming expectations about what will happen next, and when those expectations are violated, that's a learning signal. But crucially, they're not predicting at the level of every pixel on their retina. They're predicting at some more abstract level, the level of objects and their interactions, and I think that's a big part of why they can learn efficiently. That's really the intuition that motivates a lot of the work we do on self-supervised learning from video, and on things like JEPA, where you try to predict in a learned representation space rather than in the raw input space.

r001.rationale: The response says infants develop a rich model of the physical world before language, citing concepts such as object permanence, solidity, and gravity.

astra-6.text:
What I find fascinating is that children seem to develop a pretty rich understanding of the world before they can describe it in language. They have expectations about objects—how they move, how they interact, whether they continue to exist when you can’t see them. And they’re building that understanding largely through observation and interaction, rather than someone explicitly labeling everything for them.

For me, that raises an interesting question for machine learning: how much of that kind of understanding can we learn directly from sensory inputs? Language is an incredibly useful source of information, but it doesn’t have to be the starting point for every concept. Those studies motivate thinking about systems that learn representations of the world by watching it, and that can use those representations to predict what happens next.

r001.rationale: The response says children develop a rich understanding of the world before they can describe it in language, including expectations about how objects move and interact.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find fascinating is that children seem to develop a pretty rich understanding of the world before they can describe it in language. They have some intuition about objects, how they move, and what might happen when they interact. So language isn’t necessarily the thing that creates those concepts.

That raises a really interesting question for machine learning: how much can a system learn just by observing the world? If you watch an object disappear behind something and then reappear, you can start to learn that it continues to exist even when you can’t see it. There’s no label telling you that. The structure of the experience itself provides a learning signal.

I think these studies are useful because they give us examples of the kinds of understanding that can emerge without language, and they push us to think about what learning objectives might make that possible.

r001.rationale: The response says children develop understanding before they can describe things in language, including intuitions about objects, their movement, and interactions.
